walkthroughs.body_html:
Unit 4: Personal or Creative Writing and Reading Literary and Non-fiction Texts — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Unit 4: Personal or Creative Writing and Reading Literary and Non-fiction Texts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Unit 4: Personal or Creative Writing and Reading Literary and Non-fiction Texts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between transitive and intransitive verbs?
options: Transitive verbs take a direct object ('she ate the cake'); intransitive verbs don't ('she slept'). Some verbs are both depending on use ('she ran' / 'she ran the company').
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
Transitive verbs are action verbs and intransitive are linking verbs.

mcqs.q: Why does English vocabulary have so many synonyms?
options: English has many synonyms because Shakespeare invented lots of words.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
Layered historical contact — Old English, Old Norse, Norman French and Latin — left English with multiple words from different sources for similar concepts (e.g. ask/question/interrogate).
Standard English is the original and correct form of the language.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
A dialect that has gained social and institutional prestige — used in education and formal writing; it is one variety, not inherently superior in linguistic terms.
